article.overview: A broadband seismometer is designed to respond to ground motion over a wide range of frequencies, from very slow tilts and tides to the faster vibrations of nearby events. The aim is to record a complete picture of a seismic event, not just its high-frequency arrivals or its long-period drift. A 'very broadband' (VBB) instrument extends the response further toward the slowest motions. On the Moon, such instruments would help to show the deep interior: how seismic waves travel through the mantle and core, and whether the Moon has a fluid core. No broadband seismometer has been confirmed operating on the Moon in the sources reviewed for this article. The Apollo Passive Seismic Experiment used long-period and short-period sensors, not broadband ones [19]. The most advanced lunar broadband instrument with a published flight configuration is NASA's Farside Seismic Suite (FSS), whose vertical VBB seismometer was contributed by France's CNES and was originally built as a flight spare for the InSight Mars lander [1]. FSS is listed as 'Future' on NASA's mission page, and its lander assignment changed in 2026 [1][3][4]. China's Chang'e-7 lunar seismograph includes a broadband seismometer, but that mission has not launched [9][10]. NASA's Lunar Environment Monitoring Station (LEMS) has been completed and accepted for flight, but its broadband configuration is described inconsistently [11][14]. The InSight SEIS instrument, which carried a VBB sensor to Mars, is the main flown heritage for lunar broadband designs, but it is not a lunar instrument [7][8].
article.description:
A seismometer measures how the ground moves. Its 'band' is the range of frequencies it records faithfully. Broadband instruments are defined by a flat response across a wide band, rather than by a single fixed period. In the Moon's case, the lower end of the band matters for tides, large-scale structure and slow thermal motions. The upper end matters for fine detail near the surface and for local events. There is no single formal boundary for 'broadband' or 'very broadband'. Each instrument is defined by its published frequency response, and the numerical band varies from one design and one source to another.

Lunar instruments face a particular problem. Slow motions are small compared with the Earth's, and the instrument must be insensitive to thermal and mechanical disturbances from the lander and the surface. The instrument must also be compact, low-power and tolerant of a long, cold lunar night. These constraints shape the choice of sensor and enclosure. The FSS VBB, the InSight VBB and the LEMS broadband sensor are all described in the sources as seismometers designed for these conditions [1][7][13], but the sources do not give the detailed technology of each.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications:
A broadband seismometer is the standard tool for probing deep structure. Its wide band lets one instrument record both the long-period surface waves that travel around and through the Moon and the shorter-period body waves that pass through the core and mantle. Several connected goals follow from this:

- **Interior structure.** Seismic velocity and attenuation profiles constrain the thickness of the crust and mantle, and whether the core is liquid or solid. The FSS page states that its seismometers will measure far-side moonquakes and meteor impacts for the first time [1]. The VBB is the component that would extend the record to the lowest frequencies.
- **Deep moonquakes and tidal response.** Deep moonquakes are weak, long-period events, and their detection depends on a low-frequency response. This is a general seismological requirement for a lunar VBB, not a claim taken from a specific mission source in this run.
- **Far-side and polar coverage.** The FSS is intended to operate on the far side of the Moon, where no seismometer has previously operated [1]. LEMS is intended for the south polar region [14]. Coverage of different regions is a scientific reason for more than one station.
- **Calibration of the instrument itself.** Broadband instruments need extensive calibration. The Chang'e-7 team's calibration paper lists a calibration accuracy requirement of no more than 3 per cent for its sensors [9].
article.operating_principle:
The sources read for this article do not describe the internal measurement principle of the FSS, Chang'e-7 or LEMS broadband sensors in enough detail to state it for each. The general principle for very broadband seismometers is well established and is described here for orientation only. Most VBB designs use a proof mass that is suspended so that it moves very little when the ground moves. A sensor measures the motion of the proof mass relative to the frame, and a feedback loop keeps the mass near its rest position. The feedback force, or the signal needed to hold the mass, is proportional to ground acceleration, which is recorded and integrated to give velocity or displacement. Because the mass is held almost still, the response can extend to very long periods. Operation requires careful thermal control, since temperature changes can shift the balance of the suspension. Whether a particular lunar instrument uses this arrangement is not confirmed by the sources read here.

The Chang'e-7 calibration paper gives the broadband channel's measurement characteristics in requirement form: a measurement band of 1/120 to 10 Hz, a sensitivity of 2000 ± 60 V/g, a self-noise better than 2.5 × 10⁻⁹ g/√Hz at 1 Hz, and a dynamic range greater than 120 dB [9]. These are the specification values for that channel, not measured data.
article.scientific_importance: Broadband seismology is central to lunar geophysics because a single very broadband station can resolve both the deep and near-surface structure. Apollo's long-period and short-period sensors recorded the Moon's seismic activity but did not cover the full band a modern broadband instrument would. A lunar network with VBB sensors would therefore provide the first continuous, wideband record of deep moonquakes and of the lunar interior's response to tides. The FSS and LEMS missions, if flown, would be the first to extend such coverage to the far side and the south pole, respectively [1][14]. The importance of this capability is a scientific judgment; the source-based limits on what has been measured are given below.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a broadband seismometer. The instruments below differ in technology, band, axes and status, and their numbers are not directly comparable. Sources for the flown InSight VBB give a band that differs between summaries. Sources for the lunar examples are mostly requirements, design targets or press statements. Where a value is not published in the sources read, the text says so rather than estimating it.

examples.name: Farside Seismic Suite — vertical Very Broadband (VBB) seismometer
examples.type: Lunar flight hardware (built; not flown); mission status 'Future'
examples.status: Listed as 'Future' on NASA's JPL mission page. The mission was intended to fly on a Draper-led, ispace-developed CLPS lander (CP-12), whose contract was ended on 15 July 2026. The JPL page names no lander and gives no date.
examples.sensor_configuration: One vertical VBB seismometer, contributed by CNES, and one triaxial Short Period sensor [1].
examples.description: NASA's JPL page describes FSS as delivering 'two sensitive seismometers' to the far side of the Moon, and says that the VBB 'was originally constructed as a flight spare for NASA's InSight Mars lander' [1]. It is contributed by the French space agency CNES and is described as vertical. JPL calls it 'the most sensitive seismometer ever built for use in space exploration' and says it 'can detect ground motions smaller than the size of a single hydrogen atom' [1]. These are NASA's own qualitative statements, not measured values, and the page gives no frequency band, noise figure, mass, dimensions or power for the VBB. The VBB is the instrument the sources identify as the broadband element of FSS [1][2]. The FSS mission is intended to operate for 'at least 4½ months' on solar power and to provide its own power, communications and thermal control [1]. Its mission status is less clear than the JPL page suggests. A Moon Monday newsletter of 27 July 2026 reports that the Draper-led, ispace-developed CLPS mission was supposed to carry FSS [3]. ispace-U.S. says that Draper and NASA agreed to end CLPS task order CP-12, and that ispace-U.S. had been a subcontractor for that task order [4]. The ispace page does not mention FSS. The newsletter reports that the contract was cancelled and that NASA might reallocate flight-ready payloads to another lander [3]. As of 12 November 2026, no sources read give a new lander or launch date for FSS.

examples.name: InSight SEIS very broadband (VBB) sensor — Mars flight heritage
examples.type: Flown on Mars (InSight); not a lunar instrument
examples.status: Flown on NASA's InSight lander on Mars. It is cited here as the design heritage of the FSS VBB, which JPL describes as a flight spare of this instrument [1].
examples.sensor_configuration: Very broadband sensor within the SEIS package, alongside a short-period sensor.
examples.description:
InSight's SEIS seismometer was deployed on the Martian surface in December 2018 [7]. NASA's photojournal shows the instrument on the surface and under its dome [7][8]. The SEIS package contains a very broadband sensor and a short-period sensor. Two summaries of the VBB's band disagree. A DLR summary describes the VBB component as covering roughly 0.01 to 10 Hz [6]. A 2019 EGU abstract summary, seen only as a search result, gives 0.01 to 5 Hz for the VBB and about 0.01 to 50 Hz for the whole SEIS system [not fetched in full]. The VBB's mass, power and sensor technology are not stated in any source read for this article. The primary SEIS overview paper [5] could not be read in full, so its published VBB numbers are not used here.

The InSight VBB shows that a VBB seismometer can be built to survive the transport and deployment of a planetary lander, and it is the most direct engineering heritage for the FSS VBB [1]. It does not show lunar performance. The instrument's Mars data are not used in this article.

examples.name: Chang'e-7 lunar seismograph — broadband seismometer channel
examples.type: Lunar flight hardware (not yet launched); values are design requirements
examples.status: Assigned to the Chang'e-7 lander. Launch did not proceed in the planned 2026 window [10]; no new date was found in the sources read.
examples.sensor_configuration: Lunar seismograph containing a broadband seismometer and a MEMS seismometer [9].
examples.description: The Chang'e-7 calibration paper lists the required specifications for the broadband seismometer, with the MEMS sensor as a companion [9]. The broadband seismometer's measurement bandwidth is specified as 1/120 to 10 Hz, with self-noise better than 2.5 × 10⁻⁹ g/√Hz at 1 Hz, a sensitivity of 2000 ± 60 V/g and a dynamic range above 120 dB [9]. The paper specifies a calibration error of no more than 3 per cent [9]. The paper describes the instrument as designed for an eight-year operation lifetime [9]. All of these are requirements, not measured lunar performance. The paper is described as proposing a ground calibration test plan, and it reports no measured flight results [9]. Mass and power are not stated in the HTML text read for this article. The mission has not launched, and Xinhua reported on 23 August 2026 that the launch would not proceed in its planned window that year [10].

examples.name: Lunar Environment Monitoring Station (LEMS) — broadband seismometer
examples.type: Lunar flight hardware (flight-accepted; not yet assigned to a mission)
examples.status: LEMS was completed and accepted for flight in 2026 and is stored at NASA Goddard until it is assigned to an Artemis mission [14]. The mission assignment is not confirmed in the sources read.
examples.sensor_configuration: Sources differ. A 2025 abstract describes a three-axis short-period seismometer paired with a three-axis broadband seismometer [11]. A 2026 university release describes 'two sets of identical sensors' [13]. A NASA technical paper, older than the 2025 abstract and read only as a search summary, describes a Silicon Audio–based seismometer [not fetched].
examples.description: LEMS is designed as an astronaut-deployed seismic station with buried sensors. The 2025 abstract describes a three-axis broadband seismometer, buried by astronauts, alongside a short-period seismometer, for a three-month threshold mission and a two-year baseline [11]. The University of Arizona's Planetary Seismometer Lab, which partners with Silicon Audio, has published values for the short-period sensor. It does not publish a broadband specification in the sources read [12]. The university's 2026 release describes 'two sets of identical sensors' [13], which does not match the 2025 abstract. A NASA technical summary of the broadband sensor, read only as a search result, describes an earlier Silicon Audio–based design and notes that it is older than the current flight configuration [not fetched]. The broadband band, noise, mass and power for the flight LEMS unit are therefore not confirmed in the sources read. NASA completed LEMS in 2026 and stored it at Goddard [14].

examples.name: Fleet Space seismometer on Blue Ghost Mission 2 (SPIDER) — announced
examples.type: Commercial seismic station announced for a lunar landing; not flown; broadband classification not verified
examples.status: Announced to fly on Firefly's Blue Ghost Mission 2 to the far side. Most sources point to a late 2026 launch, but one Wikipedia snapshot states 2027. The mission has not flown [16][17].
examples.sensor_configuration: Described as a multi-component seismic station [16].
examples.description: Fleet Space Technologies is supplying a seismometer, called SPIDER, for Blue Ghost Mission 2. Sources describe it as a multi-component seismic station that operates on about one watt, with data handling supported through the lander [16]. Firefly states that the lander provides ongoing power and communications, allowing the instrument to record for up to 14 days [17]. The sources read do not give SPIDER's band, sensitivity, mass, axes or sensor type, and they do not classify it as broadband. It is included here because it is a second announced lunar seismometer, not because its broadband status is confirmed.

physical_specifications.other_concepts: The Lunar Geophysical Network (LGN) was proposed as a multi-station geophysics mission with broadband seismometers at several sites [15]. A Maryland-led team's broadband seismometer paper gives a low-frequency range of 0.001 to 1 Hz [15]. A second source, read only as a search result, gives a broader 0.001 to 20 Hz for the LGN's very broadband instrument. The two numbers are not reconciled, and the second source is not identified. The LGN is a concept and has not been built or flown.

status_and_technology_summary.status: Built; flight spare origin; not flown; lander unassigned

status_and_technology_summary.published_band: Reported as 0.01–10 Hz (DLR summary) and 0.01–5 Hz (EGU abstract summary); unresolved

status_and_technology_summary.technology: Multi-component seismic station; sensor type not stated

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Not publicly specified for any lunar broadband example in the sources read.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Not publicly specified for the FSS VBB, Chang'e-7 broadband channel or LEMS broadband sensor in the sources read. Mass values for other instruments are not used here.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Not publicly specified for the FSS VBB, Chang'e-7 broadband channel or LEMS broadband sensor in the sources read. SPIDER is described as operating on about one watt [16]; this is an announced value, not a flight measurement.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen:
A broadband seismometer on the lunar surface must survive and measure in conditions that are harsh but well described in general terms. The lunar day and night each last about two Earth weeks, so the instrument experiences large temperature swings that drive thermal distortion. In a vacuum there is no air convection to smooth them, and the instrument's own temperature must be controlled. The FSS page states that the suite is 'packaged as a self-sufficient payload, with independent power, communications, and thermal control' [1]. Dust, micrometeoroids and radiation also apply, but the sources read give no environmental test levels for the broadband sensors.

Mechanical coupling to the ground matters as much as thermal control. A seismometer records the motion of the ground it is connected to, so burial or firm coupling reduces the noise picked up from the lander and from surface activity. The LEMS concept uses sensors buried by astronauts for this reason [11]. Power is a practical constraint: the FSS is solar-powered and designed to operate for at least 4½ months [1], and the LEMS summary cited a solar array and battery arrangement for the lunar night [14]. These operational limits constrain the broadband instrument's duty cycle and its data volume. The sources read do not state how a lunar broadband instrument would handle a night without power.
article.limitations:
- No broadband seismometer has yet recorded the Moon in the sources reviewed. Every lunar broadband value in this article is a requirement, a design target, a press statement or a search summary, not a measured performance.
- The FSS VBB has no published band, noise, mass, dimensions or power in the sources read. The JPL page's qualitative statements ('the most sensitive seismometer ever built for use in space exploration') are NASA's own and are not independently quantified [1].
- The InSight VBB's band is reported differently by different summaries (0.01–10 Hz and 0.01–5 Hz). The primary SEIS paper could not be read in full [5][6].
- The LEMS broadband configuration is unresolved across sources [11][13].
- Lunar Geophysical Network band values disagree between two sources [15].
- The flight status of FSS is uncertain after the CP-12 change [3][4].
- Lander and launch dates for the Chang'e-7, LEMS and Blue Ghost 2 (SPIDER) instruments are uncertain or have slipped [10][14][17].
- Apollo long-period and short-period records are not broadband records, so they cannot be used to infer lunar broadband performance.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A broadband seismometer is a surface payload. Its transportation chain runs from Earth integration through launch, lunar transfer, landing, deployment, setup, and the power, data and thermal interfaces needed to operate. Sources read for this article describe the chain only for the FSS, the Chang'e-7 seismograph, LEMS and the announced SPIDER seismometer. The steps below are the general sequence for a surface payload, with source-specific statements attached. No compatibility with a named lander is asserted unless a source describes that interface.
transportation_process: Earth integration. The FSS VBB is packaged inside a 'cube within a cube' with the battery and the SP sensor, forming a self-sufficient payload [1][2]. How the package is mounted to a lander is not stated in the sources read.

Launch and cruise. The launch vehicle and cruise profile for FSS are not stated in the sources read. The planned lander for FSS is described as a Draper-led, ispace-developed CLPS lander, but that task order has been ended [3][4].

Lunar transfer and landing. JPL states that FSS will arrive at the far side 'via a lunar lander as part of NASA's CLPS initiative' [1]. The lander is not named. The Blue Ghost Mission 2 lander is described as supplying power and communications to the SPIDER seismometer during its operating window [17]; this is a description of that lander's announced service, not a verified interface with the FSS.

Deployment. The deployment method for FSS is not stated. Apollo PSE instruments were placed by astronauts [18]. LEMS is designed to be buried by astronauts [11]. The InSight SEIS package was placed on the Martian surface by the lander's robotic arm and covered with a shield [7][8].
Setup. Levelling, orientation and coupling to the regolith are necessary for any seismometer. The sources read do not describe these steps for the broadband examples.

Power and data. The FSS is solar-powered and designed to operate for at least 4½ months [1]. The LEMS summary cited solar arrays for the lunar day and a battery for the night [14]. The Blue Ghost Mission 2 lander is described as supplying ongoing power and communications for up to 14 days [17].

Thermal and mechanical interfaces. A broadband sensor must be isolated from lander vibration and thermal transients while it is operating. The sources read do not describe this interface for FSS or the Chang'e-7 seismograph.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Three methods appear in the sources. Astronaut deployment, used for Apollo and planned for LEMS, places sensors by hand and allows burial [11][18]. Robotic placement by a lander, used for InSight's SEIS on Mars, places the instrument by arm and then covers it [7][8]. Lander-delivered, lander-deployed instruments, such as the FSS and the announced SPIDER seismometer, depend on the lander's own deployment hardware, which is not described in the sources read [1][17]. The deployment method is a design choice that affects coupling, noise and the time needed to set up the instrument.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: The Apollo ALSEP was deployed by astronauts, who connected the Passive Seismic Experiment to a central station [18]. InSight's SEIS was placed on the Martian surface by a robotic arm in December 2018 [7][8]. LEMS, now completed and flight-accepted, has no deployment yet [14]. The FSS and Chang'e-7 seismographs have not reached the Moon.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility with a specific lander is verified for any broadband example in this article. For FSS, the intended lander was part of the CP-12 task order, which ispace-U.S. and Draper agreed to end [3][4]. For SPIDER, Firefly and Fleet Space describe the Blue Ghost Mission 2 lander as its carrier [16][17]; that is an announced arrangement, not a verified interface document. For Chang'e-7 and LEMS, the sources read do not name a specific compatibility document. Compatibility assessment must await an interface control document or an official mission statement.

article.historical_significance: No lunar broadband seismometer has yet recorded the Moon in the sources reviewed. The Apollo Passive Seismic Experiment established the basic model for lunar seismology with long-period and short-period sensors [18][19], and that record remains the only extended lunar seismic dataset in the sources read. A broadband instrument would extend that record to the lowest frequencies and to the far side and polar regions. InSight's VBB, which operated on Mars, shows that a VBB seismometer can be built and flown on a planetary lander [7][8]. The FSS VBB is described as a flight spare of that instrument [1]. The Chang'e-7 and LEMS broadband channels would add to the record if they fly [9][14], and the Blue Ghost Mission 2 seismometer would add a further commercial station [16][17]. The historical significance of this payload therefore depends on whether these missions fly and on how their data are published.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties:
- The broadband numbers for the FSS VBB, InSight VBB, LEMS broadband sensor and SPIDER are not published in the sources read, or are inconsistent between sources. Each unresolved value is marked 'not stated' in the table and as null in the JSON.
- The primary InSight SEIS paper [5] could not be read in full. Its VBB figures are not used.
- The FSS lander assignment and launch date are unknown after the CP-12 change. The newsletter reports that NASA might reallocate the payloads, but no reallocation was found [3][4].
- Chang'e-7 values are requirements from a calibration paper, read from HTML tables; its PDF body was not extracted [9].
- LEMS broadband configuration is inconsistent across the 2025 abstract, the 2026 university release, and an older NASA technical summary read only as a search result [11][13].
- The Lunar Geophysical Network band disagrees between two sources, one of which is an unidentified search snippet [15].
- SPIDER's band, sensitivity, mass and sensor type were not found, and its broadband status is not verified [16].
- Image descriptions for PIA22956 and PIA23177 come from search summaries and must be checked against the NASA pages before publication [7][8].
- Several references are search-result snippets or were carried over from earlier research and not re-read in this run; each is marked in the reference list.

data_quality_notes: catalogue_id is set to the catalogue payload ID (2). The v4 reference uses catalogue_id 1 for payload 001; the Explorer app does not read this field.
Payload name uses the exact catalogue spelling 'Broadband seismometer'.
No VBB band, noise, mass, dimensions or power is published in the sources read for the FSS VBB. All are null.

The SEIS overview paper (Lognonné et al. 2019, doi:10.1007/s11214-018-0574-6) could not be read: the HAL copy returned an access-denied bot-protection page, the Springer link requires login, and the CORE PDF returned 403. The InSight VBB band, noise, sensor type and mass are therefore unverified; the figures in the text are secondary summaries and conflict with each other.

The FSS lander assignment is not confirmed. The JPL page names no lander. The Moon Monday newsletter (27 July 2026) says FSS was supposed to fly on the Draper-led CP-12 mission, and ispace-U.S. says CP-12 was ended. The ispace page does not mention FSS, so the link between FSS and CP-12 rests on the newsletter alone. The newsletter says 'cancelled'; ispace says 'end'.
NASA may reallocate flight-ready payloads to another CLPS lander, according to the newsletter. No reallocation was found in the sources read.

Chang'e-7 broadband values are design requirements from Table 1 and Table 2 of the 2026 calibration paper (Chinese text, read from the HTML page). The PDF body was not extracted. The paper does not report measured performance.

LEMS broadband configuration is inconsistent across sources (three-axis broadband with SP per the 2025 abstract, versus 'two sets of identical sensors' per the 2026 release). The broadband sensor's noise, band, mass and power are not published in the sources read.
The lunar Geophysical Network broadband band is 0.001–1 Hz in one paper (search snippet) and 0.001–20 Hz in another (unidentified search snippet). Neither was read in full.

SPIDER's sensor type, band, sensitivity and mass were not found. The source calls it multi-component; it is not classified as broadband in the sources read. The launch date is late 2026 in most sources and 2027 in one Wikipedia snapshot.

Apollo context: the statement that the Apollo PSE was not broadband is based on the payload 003 and 004 research and on the Apollo 16 image caption. The Nunn et al. (2020) review was not re-read in this run.
Several reference entries were carried over from payload 003 and were not re-read in this run (see the access note for each reference).

The Wen et al. (2026) PDF was not extracted. Chang'e-7 values come from HTML tables. The Chinese table text was translated by the research agent, so exact wording should be checked against the PDF before publication.
PIA22956 and PIA23177 descriptions are taken from search summaries of NASA pages and should be checked against the pages before publication. The two pages spell the SEIS acronym differently.

Image rights: PIA images are credited to NASA/JPL-Caltech; NASA's general policy suggests they are public domain, but the rights of each image were not checked individually. The Chang'e-7 diagram is a journal figure whose licence was not verified.

Automated HTTP check on 2026-11-12: the three PIA images, the Chang'e-7 diagram and the LEMS image returned HTTP 200 with an image content type (the Apollo 16 image is checked in the validation step). Source pages were read through web-fetch summaries or search results; several references are search-result snippets only (see access notes).
Mission status statements reflect sources available on 2026-11-12. Mission dates, lander assignments and launch dates may change quickly.
